title: Higher Than Elephant Hill, Rougher Too: Planning a Kinangop Hike in the Aberdares
meta_title: Kinangop Hike: 3,906 m of Wild Aberdare Moorland
meta_description: Plan a Kinangop hike to the Aberdares' 3,906 m second summit: Njabini and Mutarakwa routes, trail stats, KWS ranger, best months and kit from Nairobi.
excerpt: A Kinangop hike climbs the Aberdares' second-highest peak at 3,906 m, usually via Elephant Hill from Njabini: about 28 km and 10-12 hours, or two days. Here are the routes, season, ranger rules and kit, plus how to get there from Nairobi.

content:
At 3,906 m, Mt Kinangop is the second-highest peak in the Aberdares, and a Kinangop hike is one of the longest, wildest days out within 100 km of Nairobi. Most groups start at Njabini Forest Station, cross Elephant Hill and the open moorland beyond, and cover about 28 km in 10-12 hours, or split it over two days.

Many Nairobi hikers know Elephant Hill; fewer carry on to the bigger summit north of it, because the route is longer, wetter and poorly marked. Below are both main routes, trail stats, the best months, the KWS escort, kit and training.

Quick Facts

  • Summit: Mt Kinangop, 3,906 m, the second-highest point of the Aberdare Range after Ol Donyo Lesatima.
  • Location: southern Aberdares, Nyandarua County, inside Aberdare National Park.
  • Main start points: Njabini Forest Station (about 2,500 m) or Mutarakwa Forest Station (about 2,600 m).
  • Distance and time: about 28 km from Njabini via Elephant Hill; 10-12 hours in one day, or two days with a moorland camp.
  • Elevation gain: roughly 1,600 m of climbing in total.
  • Escort: an armed Kenya Wildlife Service ranger is required, as elephants and buffalo use the forest.

Where Is Mt Kinangop and How Do You Get There From Nairobi?

Mt Kinangop rises at the southern end of the Aberdare Range in Nyandarua County, roughly 90-110 km north-west of Nairobi depending on the trailhead. The drive takes about two to two and a half hours, so an early start is the only way to finish a Kinangop hike in daylight.

Driving to Njabini

Take the Nairobi-Nakuru highway up the escarpment for about 60 km to the "flyover" junction, then turn towards the Kinangop plateau and follow the tarmac for about 24 km to Njabini town. Njabini Forest Station, where most people begin a Kinangop hike, is about 4 km further on murram that turns slippery after rain.

Driving to Mutarakwa

For the north-western approach, continue past Njabini on the Ol Kalou road to Engineer, then follow dirt roads for about 7 km to Mutarakwa Forest Station. It adds about 20 km of driving for a quieter Kinangop hike.

Can you get there by matatu?

Only as far as the towns. Matatus run from central Nairobi to Njabini and to Ndunyu Njeru via Engineer; confirm the current stage before you travel. A boda boda then covers the last 4-7 km. Because of the dawn start, most groups share a car.

Kinangop Hike Routes Compared

There are two well-used ways up. The Njabini route links Elephant Hill and Kinangop along the high ridge, while the Mutarakwa route climbs from the north-west through older indigenous forest. Both versions of the Kinangop hike need a KWS ranger, and both reward a two-day plan unless you walk fast.

Some groups traverse from Njabini to Mutarakwa with a car waiting at the far end. Treat every figure here as approximate: your pace on wet ground decides the day.

What Is the Kinangop Hike Like, Stage by Stage?

The route passes through five vegetation belts in a single day: plantation forest, indigenous forest, bamboo, giant heather and open moorland. The climbing is steady rather than technical until the summit block, where a short rocky section needs hands as well as feet.

Plantation forest and farms

The first few kilometres follow forest roads through plantations, where farmers grow potatoes and cabbages between young trees. It is easy walking.

The bamboo belt

From around 2,800 m the path enters dense bamboo, and this is where a Kinangop hike turns muddy. Animal trails close in overhead, the ground stays wet most of the year and boots sink to the ankle. On the Mutarakwa side, guides sometimes clear overgrown sections with a panga.

Elephant Hill and the moorland

On the Njabini route you first top out on Elephant Hill at about 3,600 m, then drop around 200 m onto the moorland. Tussock grass, giant lobelias and senecios take over, with spongy bogs between volcanic knolls. Buffalo paths lead up the final ridge.

The summit block

Kinangop has two tops, about 3,906 m and 3,864 m. The final 30 m or so to the higher one is a steep rock scramble, the only part of a Kinangop hike where you need your hands. In fog or rain, stop below it unless your guide is confident. On a clear morning you see Mt Kenya to the east, Table Mountain to the north and Longonot towards the Rift Valley.

When Is the Best Time for a Kinangop Hike?

The driest months are usually January to February and June to September. The long rains (roughly March to May) and the short rains (roughly October to December) turn the bamboo into a mud slide and the moorland into knee-deep bog.

Even in a dry month, expect cold. Afternoon highs on the moorland can sit around 15°C in the cooler season, and dawns drop to just above freezing. Fog rolls in within minutes and afternoon lightning storms are common, so be off the summit by early afternoon.

Planning a Kinangop hike in November or December? Allow extra time, pack full rain gear and agree a turnaround time with your guide before you set off.

Do You Need a KWS Ranger and Permit?

Yes. Every Kinangop hike enters Aberdare National Park, so you pay park entry and ranger fees and must walk with an armed Kenya Wildlife Service ranger. Elephants and buffalo use the same forest paths you will.

Arrange the ranger in advance through KWS, and confirm current fees and payment methods with Kenya Wildlife Service's Aberdare National Park page before you go. Rangers provide security, not navigation, so bring a local guide or a GPS track. Signal is patchy up there, so leave your plan with someone at home.

What to Wear and Pack for the Kinangop Hike

Pack for cold, wet mountain weather even if Nairobi is warm when you leave. The basics are waterproof boots with deep lugs, gaiters for the bamboo mud, warm layers, gloves and a full waterproof shell, plus a headlamp in case the descent runs late.

  • Boots: a waterproof mid-cut like the Quechua waterproof hiking boot keeps feet drier in the bogs and supports ankles on the scramble.
  • Gaiters: waterproof leg gaiters stop bamboo mud from pouring over your boot tops.
  • Socks: two pairs of merino wool hiking socks, so you can change into a dry pair at the summit.
  • Hands: Thinsulate waterproof gloves for the cold, wet rock near the top.
  • Light: a rechargeable headlamp, because a 12-hour Kinangop hike often ends in the dark.
  • Layers: a quick-dry base, a fleece, an insulated jacket and a hooded rain shell.
  • Food and water: 2-3 litres, a filter for stream water and plenty of snacks.

For an overnight trip, add a tent, a sleeping bag with a comfort rating close to freezing, a warm hat and a stove. Pro Tips

  • Leave Nairobi by 5:00 am so the Kinangop hike starts by about 7:30 am.
  • Set a firm turnaround time, for example 1:00 pm, and stick to it even if the summit looks close.
  • Keep a dry base layer and socks in a sealed bag for the summit or camp.

How Hard Is It, and How Should You Train?

A Kinangop hike is hard mainly because of its length, mud and altitude rather than technical difficulty. If you finished Elephant Hill with energy left, you are ready to try it; if Elephant Hill wiped you out, build up first.

  1. Start with the ridges: repeat the Ngong Hills traverse with a loaded pack until 15 km feels comfortable.
  2. Add a steep climb: the crater rim of Mt Longonot builds the legs you need for the climb out of the bamboo.
  3. Do Elephant Hill first: the Elephant Hill hike covers the first half of the Kinangop hike from Njabini and shows how your boots cope with the mud.
  4. Practise a long day: one 10-hour outing makes 12 hours on the moorland less of a shock.

Once Kinangop is done, the natural next step is Ol Donyo Lesatima, the range's highest point. Our round-up of the best hikes in Kenya shows how the Aberdare peaks compare with Mt Kenya and the Rift Valley volcanoes.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does the Kinangop hike take?

From Njabini Forest Station via Elephant Hill, the round trip to Mt Kinangop is about 28 km and takes most fit groups 10 to 12 hours. Many hikers split it into two days, walking about six hours to a moorland camp and summiting the next morning. The Mutarakwa route also usually takes two days.

Is Kinangop harder than Elephant Hill?

Yes, in most cases. Mt Kinangop stands roughly 250-280 m higher than Elephant Hill, and the Njabini route crosses Elephant Hill first, so you do all of that climb and then several more hours on the moorland. The summit also has a short, steep rock scramble that Elephant Hill lacks.

Can I do the Kinangop hike as a day trip from Nairobi?

Mt Kinangop works as a long day trip from Nairobi if you leave by 5:00 am, walk strongly and turn back on time. With about two hours' drive each way and 10-12 hours on foot, the day runs close to 16 hours. Slower groups, or anyone hiking in the rains, should camp overnight instead.

How cold does it get at the top?

The Aberdare moorland around Mt Kinangop is cold all year. Afternoon highs on the moorland are often around 15°C or lower, wind and fog make it feel colder, and nights fall to around freezing. Pack a fleece, insulated jacket, shell, gloves and warm hat, even when Nairobi is sunny.

Do you need a guide to hike Kinangop?

An armed KWS ranger is compulsory inside Aberdare National Park, but rangers are there for safety, not route-finding. The trail through the bamboo and across the moorland is poorly marked, so going with a local guide who knows Mt Kinangop, or carrying a reliable GPS track, makes a real difference, especially when fog comes in.

Final Thoughts

Two summits, bamboo and some of central Kenya's wildest moorland sit within a morning's drive of the city. Treat the Kinangop hike as a long mountain day: start before dawn, walk with a ranger and a guide, and turn back when the weather says so.
